# Hypopituitarism

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Hypothalamus and pituitary gland disorders > Hypopituitarism*

[Original Article Link](/library/-T0Dt2)

---

## Summary

Hypopituitarism refers to the inadequate production of one or more <u>anterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u> as a result of damage to the <u>pituitary gland</u> and/or <u>hypothalamus</u>. These <u>hormones</u> include <u>growth hormone</u> (<u>GH</u>), <u>prolactin</u>, <u>thyroid</u> stimulating <u>hormone</u> (<u>TSH</u>), <u>adrenocorticotropic hormone</u> (<u>ACTH</u>), <u>follicle stimulating hormone</u> (<u>FSH</u>), and <u>luteinizing hormone</u> (<u>LH</u>). In some cases, the <u>posterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u> (e.g., <u>ADH</u>) may also be affected, which is known as <u>panhypopituitarism</u>. The most common cause of hypopituitarism is compression of the <u>pituitary gland</u> by a nonsecretory <u>pituitary macroadenoma</u>. Other common causes include <u>postpartum pituitary necrosis</u> (<u>Sheehan syndrome</u>), <u>traumatic brain injury</u>, hypophysectomy, and/or <u>irradiation</u> of the <u>pituitary gland</u>. Clinical manifestations vary significantly and depend on the specific <u>hormone</u> deficiency, the age of disease onset, the rate at which hypopituitarism develops, and the underlying cause of hypopituitarism: <u>Growth hormone deficiency</u> during childhood manifests with delayed growth, while <u>prolactin</u> deficiency in women can manifest as lactation failure. Deficiencies of other <u>anterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u>, on the other hand, manifest with clinical features of <u>hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u>, <u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>, and/or <u>secondary adrenal insufficiency</u> (<u>AI</u>). Severe <u>pituitary</u> damage can also result in <u>central diabetes insipidus</u> as a result of <u>ADH</u> deficiency. Hypopituitarism is diagnosed by measuring specific <u>hormone</u> levels (depending on the underlying <u>hormone</u> deficiency) and with <u>cranial</u> imaging (in order to identify damage to the <u>pituitary gland</u> and/or <u>hypothalamus</u>). Treatment consists of <u>hormone replacement therapy</u> and treatment of the underlying disorder (e.g., <u>transsphenoidal resection</u> of <u>pituitary adenomas</u>).

---

## Etiology

* Intrasellar/parasellar masses 

* Nonsecretory <u>pituitary macroadenomas</u> (â¥ 10 mm in diameter) are the most common cause of hypopituitarism among adults.

* Less common:  <u>meningiomas</u>, <u>craniopharyngiomas</u>, <u>internal carotid artery</u> <u>aneurysms</u>, Rathke cleft cyst (a benign, intrasellar/suprasellar cyst that arises from the remnants of the <u>Rathke pouch</u>)

* Pituitary apoplexy

* <u>Infarction</u> of the <u>pituitary gland</u> as a result of <u>ischemia</u> and/or hemorrhage

* Most commonly occurs in patients with a preexisting <u>pituitary adenoma</u>

* Primarily affects the <u>anterior pituitary gland</u> because it receives its blood supply from a relatively low-pressure arterial system and is, therefore, vulnerable to <u>ischemia</u> and <u>infarction</u>.

* Sheehan syndrome: postpartum <u>necrosis</u> of the <u>pituitary gland</u>. Usually occurs following <u>postpartum hemorrhage</u>, but can also occur even without clinical evidence of hemorrhage. [[1]](/library/Zo0Z0S)[[2]](/library/sL0t_g)

* During <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>hypertrophy</u> of <u>prolactin</u>-producing regions increases the size of the <u>pituitary gland</u>, making it very sensitive to <u>ischemia</u>.

* Blood loss during delivery/<u>postpartum hemorrhage</u>;  → <u>hypovolemia</u> → vasospasm of hypophyseal vessels → <u>ischemia</u> of the <u>pituitary gland</u> → <u>empty sella</u> turcica on imaging [[3]](/library/fIXkXz)

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u> (especially around the <u>skull base</u>)

* Infiltration of the <u>pituitary</u> and/or <u>hypothalamus</u>

* <u>Hemochromatosis</u>

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Lymphocytic</u> histiocytosis

* <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>

* Infections: <u>meningitis</u>, <u>TB</u>, <u>tertiary syphilis</u>, <u>toxoplasmosis</u>, fungi (e.g., <u>histoplasmosis</u>)

* <u>Empty sella syndrome</u>

* Congenital deficiency of <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>hormones</u>

* <u>GnRH</u> deficiency (<u>Kallmann syndrome</u>)

* <u>Prader-Willi syndrome</u>

* Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> 

* Hypophysectomy

* <u>Pituitary</u> <u>irradiation</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* Hypopituitarism becomes symptomatic when more than 80% of <u>pituitary</u> cells are damaged. [[4]](/library/bo0H0S)

* In most cases, hypopituitarism develops slowly (e.g., <u>adenomas</u>, postirradiation)  [[5]](/library/U30b3f)

* Certain cases of hypopituitarism develop rapidly (e.g., <u>pituitary apoplexy</u>).

* Hypopituitarism refers to deficiency of one or more <u>anterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u> (see “<u>General endocrinology</u>“)

* GH deficiency → growth retardation (during childhood), ↓ <u>bone density</u>, muscle <u>atrophy</u>, <u>hypercholesterolemia</u>

* <u>Prolactin</u> deficiency → lactation failure following delivery

* <u>FSH</u>/<u>LH</u> deficiency → <u>hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u> (<u>secondary hypogonadism</u>)

* <u>TSH</u> deficiency → <u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>ACTH</u> deficiency → <u>secondary adrenal insufficiency</u>

* In addition to the aforementioned <u>hormone</u> deficiencies, patients with severe <u>pituitary</u> damage (panhypopituitarism) also present with deficiencies of <u>posterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u>:

* <u>ADH</u> deficiency → central <u>diabetes insipidus</u>

* <u>Oxytocin</u> deficiency → no effect

---

## Clinical features

Symptoms are variable and depend on the specific <u>hormone</u> deficiency, the age of disease onset, the rate at which hypopituitarism develops, and the underlying cause of hypopituitarism.




* General symptoms: Intrasellar/parasellar masses (e.g., <u>pituitary macroadenomas</u>, <u>craniopharyngiomas</u>) can manifest with <u>headache</u>, <u>visual field</u> defects (<u>bitemporal hemianopsia</u>), and/or <u>diplopia</u>.

* <u>Pituitary apoplexy</u> manifests with acute onset of:

* Severe <u>headache</u>

* Hypopituitarism

* Bilateral <u>hemianopia</u>, <u>diplopia</u> (due to damage to <u>CN III</u>)

* Sudden <u>hypotension</u>, possibly <u>shock</u>

* <u>GH deficiency</u>

* During childhood: <u>short stature</u>

* During adulthood

* Usually asymptomatic

* Subtle findings include weight gain, <u>weakness</u>, and <u>depression</u>.

* <u>Prolactin</u> deficiency

* Women: lactation failure following delivery

* Men: asymptomatic

* <u>FSH</u>/<u>LH</u> deficiency

* Women: <u>primary amenorrhea</u> (<u>delayed puberty</u>), <u>secondary amenorrhea</u>, irregular <u>menstrual cycles</u>, <u>infertility</u>

* Men: <u>delayed puberty</u>, loss of libido, <u>infertility</u>, testicular <u>atrophy</u>, loss of facial, axillary and/or pubic <u>hair</u>, <u>gynecomastia</u>

* <u>TSH</u> deficiency: weight gain, cold intolerance, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>constipation</u>, dry <u>skin</u> (see “<u>Hypothyroidism</u>”)

* <u>ACTH</u> deficiency: weight loss, <u>weakness</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, chronic <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypoglycemia</u> (see “<u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>”)

* <u>Central diabetes insipidus</u>: <u>polyuria</u>, <u>polydipsia</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Pituitary apoplexy</u>, which results in acute <u>hypocortisolism</u> and <u>hypothyroidism</u>, can manifest with severe <u>headache</u>, sudden <u>hypotension</u>, and <u>hypovolemic shock</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[6]](/library/HVXKDC)




* Each <u>hormone</u> deficiency must be tested individually because the pattern of <u>hormone</u> deficiency may vary.

* All patients: Assess for deficiencies of <u>ACTH</u>, <u>TSH</u>, <u>LH</u>/<u>FSH</u>, and <u>ADH</u>.

* <u>GH deficiency</u> testing: Perform if treatment is indicated (e.g., in children) or if < 3 of the other deficiency tests are positive.

* <u>Prolactin</u> testing: not routinely performed for hypopituitarism

* <u>Melanocyte stimulating hormone</u> (<u>MSH</u>) and <u>oxytocin</u> levels: not used in the diagnosis of hypopituitarism

* If a <u>hormone</u> deficiency is identified, <u>cranial</u> imaging (preferably <u>MRI</u>) is indicated to identify the cause (e.g., <u>pituitary adenoma</u>).

* In an emergency setting (e.g., <u>adrenal crisis</u>, <u>myxedema coma</u>), treatment is indicated prior to biochemical testing.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[6]](/library/HVXKDC)




#### <u>ACTH</u> deficiency (central/<u>secondary adrenal insufficiency</u>) [[7]](/library/GdXBrC)




* First line: morning <u>cortisol</u> level 

* < 3 mcg/dL: diagnosis of <u>AI</u> supported; serum <u>ACTH</u> values required to differentiate between primary and central <u>AI</u> 

* High <u>ACTH</u>: supports primary <u>AI</u>

* Low to normal <u>ACTH</u>: supports central <u>AI</u>

* 3–15 mcg/dL: Perform <u>ACTH stimulation test</u>.

* > 15 mcg/dL: likely excludes <u>AI</u>

* For further information on the diagnosis of <u>secondary adrenal insufficiency</u>, see “<u>Endocrine testing for adrenal insufficiency</u>.”





#### <u>TSH</u> deficiency (<u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>)




* First line: <u>thyroid function tests</u> (both <u>TSH</u> and free T4 are required)

* Supportive findings: ↓ or normal <u>TSH</u> with ↓ serum free T4 and ↓ serum free T3

* For further information on the diagnosis of <u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>, see “Diagnostics” in “<u>Hypothyroidism</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> A normal <u>TSH</u> does not rule out <u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>; always send for serum free T4 levels.




#### <u>LH</u>/<u>FSH</u> deficiency (<u>secondary hypogonadism</u>)




* Men

* <u>Testosterone</u>: ↓

* <u>LH</u> and <u>FSH</u>: ↓

* <u>DHEA</u> (if sent): ↓

* Women

* Patients with regular <u>menstrual cycles</u>: confirms normal <u>gonadotropin</u> function; no further diagnostic testing required

* Routine testing in <u>oligomenorrhea</u>, <u>amenorrhea</u>, or <u>postmenopause</u> if <u>secondary hypogonadism</u> is suspected:

* <u>Estradiol</u>: ↓

* <u>LH</u> and <u>FSH</u>: ↓

* For other causes of <u>oligomenorrhea</u> or <u>amenorrhea</u>, see “<u>Diagnostics for abnormal uterine bleeding</u>” and “<u>Diagnostics for amenorrhea</u>.”

* For further information on the diagnosis of <u>secondary hypogonadism</u>, see “Diagnostics” in “<u>Hypogonadism</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> The presence of regular <u>menstrual cycles</u> in women rules out <u>hypogonadism</u>.




#### <u>Growth hormone deficiency</u>




* Testing is required if treatment is planned and optional if treatment is not planned and hormonal deficiencies exist in ≥ 3 <u>pituitary</u> axes.

* <u>IGF-1</u> level: typically ↓; may be normal  [[8]](/library/cUXaXx)

* <u>Confirmatory testing</u>: GH stimulation test   [[8]](/library/cUXaXx)[[9]](/library/eUXxXx)

* Procedure 

* Record baseline serum <u>GH</u> level.

* Administer stimulating agent (e.g., macimorelin).

* Repeat serum <u>GH</u> levels at set intervals.

* Interpretation: ↓ <u>GH</u> level (e.g., level < 2.8 mcg/L post macimorelin stimulation) supports a <u>GH deficiency</u>.  [[9]](/library/eUXxXx)





#### <u>Prolactin</u> deficiency




* Routine testing is not performed in the investigation of hypopituitarism.

* <u>Prolactin</u> levels may be tested in:

* Isolated <u>prolactin</u> deficiency

* Men with low <u>testosterone</u> levels to rule out a <u>prolactinoma</u>

* Supportive finding: low-normal to low <u>prolactin</u> level, which does not increase with stimulation testing  [[10]](/library/QUXu1x)





#### <u>Posterior pituitary</u> <u>hormones</u>: <u>ADH</u> deficiency (<u>central diabetes insipidus</u>)




* Initial testing

* 24-hour urine collection: ↑ urine volume, ↓ <u>urine osmolality</u>

* <u>Plasma osmolality</u>: ↑ or normal  [[11]](/library/4UX3Wx)

* Serum <u>sodium</u>: ↑ or normal

* <u>Water deprivation test</u> 

* Initial deprivation: no change to <u>urine osmolality</u>

* Following <u>exogenous</u> <u>desmopressin</u> administration: increased <u>urine osmolality</u>

* For further information, see “<u>Diagnostic workup of diabetes insipidus</u>.”





![Diagnostic approach to suspected arginine vasopressin disorder (diabetes insipidus)](media/mkpninuylcjkf8ywnsxn7cqd.jpg)

Diagnostic approach to suspected arginine vasopressin disorder (diabetes insipidus)




### Imaging [[12]](/library/OUXIWx)




Imaging of the <u>pituitary</u> is indicated in all patients to determine the underlying cause.




* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>

* Preferred imaging modality

* Findings depend on the underlying etiology and include <u>pituitary adenomas</u> (most common cause in adults), congenital <u>malformations</u>, and trauma.

* CT Head (without IV contrast): used if there are <u>contraindications to MRI</u> or in patients requiring rapid evaluation, e.g., after suspected <u>TBI</u> or <u>SAH</u>

## Treatment

### Approach [[6]](/library/HVXKDC)




* Assess patients for signs of clinical instability and, if present, initiate emergency management.

* All patients require <u>pituitary</u> <u>hormone</u> replacement to treat the conditions that result from hypopituitarism.

* Treat all patients for <u>secondary adrenal insufficiency</u>, <u>secondary hypothyroidism</u>, <u>hypogonadism</u>, and <u>diabetes insipidus</u>.

* Treat <u>growth hormone deficiency</u> in all children and consider treatment in adults.

* No treatment is indicated for deficiencies of <u>prolactin</u>, <u>oxytocin</u>, or <u>MSH</u>.

* Identify and treat the underlying cause (e.g., <u>transsphenoidal resection</u> in some cases of <u>pituitary macroadenomas</u>).

* Ensure patients receive appropriate education on the following aspects:

* Importance of <u>treatment adherence</u>

* Effects of intercurrent illness (e.g., sick days rules in <u>adrenal insufficiency</u>)

* Need for an emergency bracelet or necklace





### Emergency management




Acute loss of <u>pituitary</u> function, e.g., via <u>pituitary apoplexy</u> (including <u>Sheehan syndrome</u>), <u>iatrogenic</u> (hypophysectomy), or <u>traumatic brain injury</u>, can lead to life-threatening complications.




* <u>Adrenal crisis</u>: Give immediate IV <u>hydrocortisone</u> without waiting for diagnostic confirmation (see “<u>Adrenal crisis</u>” for dosage information).

* <u>Myxedema coma</u>

* Give IV <u>hydrocortisone</u> because of the risk of <u>levothyroxine</u> precipitating an <u>adrenal crisis</u> through enhanced clearance of <u>cortisol</u>.

* Replace <u>thyroid hormones</u> via IV <u>levothyroxine</u> and <u>liothyronine</u>.

* See “<u>Myxedema</u> <u>Coma</u>” for dosages.

* <u>Hypernatremia</u>

* Start <u>desmopressin</u> (see “Treatment” in “<u>Diabetes</u> Insipidus”).

* <u>Replace free water deficit</u> (see “Treatment” in “<u>Hypernatremia</u>” for further management).

* Once stabilized, patients should be started on maintenance <u>pituitary</u> <u>hormone</u> replacement.





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with suspected <u>adrenal crisis</u> require immediate therapy with <u>hydrocortisone</u>.




### <u>Maintenance therapy</u> for <u>pituitary</u> <u>hormone</u> deficiencies




| <br><u>Hormone</u> replacement in hypopituitarism [[6]](/library/HVXKDC) |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Secondary adrenal insufficiency</u> | <br>* Routine management: <u>glucocorticoids</u> with dose increases during periods of <u>stress</u><br><br> |
| <u>Secondary hypothyroidism</u> | <br><br>* New diagnosis: Rule out <u>ACTH</u> deficiency before starting treatment, as <u>levothyroxine</u> increases the clearance of <u>cortisol</u> and may precipitate an <u>adrenal crisis</u>. [[13]](/library/meXVzC)<br><br>* Routine management: <u>levothyroxine</u><br><br>* Monitor treatment <u>efficacy</u> with free T4 levels (not <u>TSH</u>).<br><br><br> |
| <u>Secondary hypogonadism</u> | <br><br>* Men<br><br>* <u>Testosterone</u> replacement  [[14]](/library/ShXyWB)<br><br>* If <u>fertility</u> is desired, <u>exogenous</u> <u>gonadotropins</u> (e.g., <u>hCG</u>) [[15]](/library/4hX3VB)<br><br>* Females: <u>estrogen</u> replacement with <u>progesterone</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Growth hormone deficiency</u> [[8]](/library/cUXaXx) | <br><br>* Children: <u>growth hormone</u> replacement  [[16]](/library/_gX5Bx)<br><br>* Adults: <u>GH</u> replacement may be offered but is not usually required.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Central diabetes insipidus</u> | <br>* Routine management: <u>desmopressin</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> In addition to <u>pituitary</u> <u>hormone</u> replacement, the underlying cause of hypopituitarism should be treated.




> [!WARNING]
> Hypopituitarism patients with <u>TSH</u> deficiency should not be treated with <u>levothyroxine</u> until <u>ACTH</u> deficiency has been ruled out and/or treated because <u>levothyroxine</u> increases the clearance of <u>cortisol</u> and may precipitate an <u>adrenal crisis</u>.
